h1: Rice lagers of Asia compared from Japan to Thailand and India
title: Asian Rice Lagers Compared | Craft Beer School
desc: How rice lagers from Japan, Thailand, Vietnam, China and India differ, why brewers use rice and what to look for when you taste them side by side.
teaser: Japan's dry lagers, Thailand's beach beers and India's strong beers all use rice. They taste nothing alike.
standfirst: Across Asia, the everyday beer is a pale lager brewed with rice. That shared ingredient hides a lot of variety. Here is how rice lagers differ from Japan to India and why.
sections:
Rice is mostly starch with very little protein or oil. Brewed alongside barley malt, it adds fermentable sugar without adding much flavour or colour. The beer comes out lighter in body, paler and crisper than an all malt lager. Rice also lowers the protein that can cause haze, so the beer stays bright for longer.

Rice is local and often cheaper than imported malt in much of Asia, which helped its spread. But it is also a flavour choice. A well made rice lager is meant to be clean, dry and refreshing in heat and humidity. Our guide to rice and maize adjuncts explains how brewers use them in India.

Rice starch gelatinises at higher temperatures than barley starch, so most breweries boil the rice in a separate cereal cooker before adding it to the main mash, where enzymes from the malt convert it to sugar.

Japanese rice lagers are usually pale, very clear and highly attenuated, which means the yeast converts almost all the sugar. The result is a dry, crisp beer with a short finish. Some brands market this as karakuchi, or dry. Hop aroma is light and malt is subtle. These beers are designed to sit next to food such as yakitori, tempura or sushi without getting in the way.

Japanese tax law separates beer from lower malt categories such as happoshu, which has shaped what brewers make and what they call it. When you taste a Japanese lager, look for brilliance, a clean grain note and very little sweetness.

Southeast Asian lagers tend to be light, fizzy and served very cold, often over ice in Thailand and Vietnam. Rice gives a light body. Most are moderate in alcohol with low bitterness. They are built for street food, heat and long evenings.

Vietnam also has a draught culture of very fresh, light beer poured from kegs on the street, known as bia hoi. Chinese mass market lagers are often light in body and pale, frequently brewed with rice, with a soft grain flavour. Strength and bitterness vary by brand and region.
India: strong beer and the adjunct mix

India's mass market lager follows a different path. The category many Indian drinkers reach for is strong beer, usually 5 to 8% ABV. Brewers here use rice, maize or sugar as adjuncts, depending on cost and availability. Many breweries use high gravity brewing, where a stronger wort is fermented and then diluted with deaerated water before packaging.

Strong Indian lagers often taste sweeter and fuller than Japanese ones, with more alcohol warmth and a little grain. Lighter Indian lagers, around 4.5 to 5%, are closer to the Southeast Asian model. Craft brewers in India also use local rice varieties in some beers, which is worth looking out for on taproom menus.
How they compare with Western lagers

American mass market lager also uses rice or corn. Our guide to American light lager covers that cousin. German lagers such as helles are traditionally all malt, which gives them a rounder, bready flavour and fuller body. Tasting a helles next to a Japanese rice lager is a quick lesson in what rice actually does: less bread, less body, more snap.

If you can find a few, line them up at the same temperature, around 4 to 6 °C. Look first at clarity and colour. Then notice body: how thin or full the beer feels. Then the finish: does it stop short and dry, or linger sweet? Strong Indian beers will show alcohol warmth that the others lack.

Rice lagers are often dismissed as plain. They are hard to brew well, because a clean, light beer has nothing to hide a fault behind. A trace of sulphur, a cooked corn note from DMS or a stale cardboard edge stands out. Learning to spot those small differences is a good test of any palate.
Why the style matters for India

Rice lagers are the beer most Indians grew up with. Knowing how they are built and why a strong beer tastes the way it does makes it easier to appreciate the craft styles that sit beside them on a taproom board. It also explains a lot about brewing in a hot country, where a crisp, light beer is often exactly what people want.
faqs: Why do Asian lagers use rice?
Rice adds fermentable sugar without much flavour or protein, making beer paler, lighter and crisper. It is also widely available across Asia.
Is Indian strong beer made with rice?
Many Indian lagers use rice, maize or sugar as adjuncts. The choice varies by brewery and changes with cost and supply.
Does rice make beer taste of rice?
Not much. Rice mainly lightens body and colour. The flavour stays clean and slightly grainy.
